title: Estimating Volume
keyIdea: Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up. It is measured in cubic centimetres (cm³): one centimetre cube is 1 cm³. To find the volume of a cuboid without counting every cube, count the cubes in one layer, then multiply by the number of layers. To estimate, round each edge to an easy whole number first, or compare with benchmarks you know: a centimetre cube is 1 cm³, a matchbox is about 25 cm³ and a litre carton is about 1,000 cm³. Capacity is how much a container holds: 1,000 cm³ of water is 1 litre, so 1 cm³ holds 1 ml.
familyTip: Fill a small box with dice, sugar cubes or Lego bricks: count one layer, then the layers. Then guess the volume of a cereal box, a mug and a shoebox before measuring. To check capacity, fill a bucket or saucepan from a 1 litre jug and count the jugfuls.

visual.caption: Is each estimate sensible? Drag each card, or tap it and then a box.

items: A 10 cm cube of water: 1 litre

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build blocks from cm cubes, fill a box in layers, sort objects, round edges and pour a litre.

kid: Volume is how much space something takes up. We measure it with small cubes that are 1 cm along each edge. One of these cubes is 1 cubic centimetre, written 1 cm³. A block made of 12 cubes has a volume of 12 cm³. Two blocks can look very different and still have the same volume. A tall block and a long flat block can both be made of 12 cubes. Do not judge by how tall or long it looks. Count the cubes.
You do not need to count every cube. Count the cubes that cover the bottom of a box. That is one layer. Then count how many layers fit on top. A layer of 20 cubes, 3 layers high, is 60 cubes.

To estimate, compare with things you know. A centimetre cube is 1 cm³, a matchbox is about 25 cm³, and a litre carton of juice is about 1,000 cm³. For a box, round each edge to an easy number first, then work out a layer and the layers.
Capacity is how much a container can hold. A box 10 cm each way holds 1,000 cm³ of water. That is exactly 1 litre, so 1 cm³ of water is 1 ml.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. This is the Year 5 measurement statement in the National Curriculum in England: estimate volume (for example, using 1 cm³ blocks to build cuboids, including cubes) and capacity (for example, using water). It prepares for the Year 6 statements on calculating volume and for the Common Core grade 5 standards 5.MD.C.3 and 5.MD.C.4 (volume as unit cubes packed without gaps or overlaps, measured in cubic cm).

The lab builds two blocks of 12 cubes with different shapes, fills a 5 × 4 × 3 box one row then one layer at a time, sorts eight objects into volume bands using benchmarks, rounds a 9.8 × 5.1 × 4.2 cm box to 10 × 5 × 4 to estimate about 200 cm³ (exact 209.9 cm³), and fills a 10 cm cube with water to show 1,000 cm³ = 1 litre.

Common mistakes. Children judge volume by height or length alone, add the edge lengths (5 + 4 + 3 = 12) instead of counting layers, count only one layer or only the faces they can see, use cm or cm² for volume, and make estimates that are wildly off because they have no benchmark. Ask them to say what one cube, one layer and one litre look like before they estimate.

practice.prompt: A box is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm tall. How many 1 cm cubes fill it?
practice.hint: Find how many cubes cover the bottom, then how many layers stack up.
practice.explain: One layer is 5 × 4 = 20 cubes, and 3 layers make 60. 12 is 5 + 4 + 3, which adds the edges instead of counting cubes.

practice.prompt: One layer of a box holds {a} cubes. The box is {b} layers tall. What is its volume in cm³?
practice.hint: Each layer has {a} cubes. Add a layer {b} times, or work out {a} × {b}.
practice.explain: {a} cubes a layer × {b} layers = {=a*b} cubes, so the volume is {=a*b} cm³.

practice.prompt: Which is the best estimate for the volume of a hen's egg?
practice.hint: Compare with a matchbox (about 25 cm³) and a litre carton (about 1,000 cm³).
practice.explain: An egg is about two matchboxes, so about 50 to 60 cm³. 5 cm³ is smaller than a dice, and 5,000 cm³ is five litre cartons.

practice.prompt: A box is about {l} cm long, 5 cm wide and 2 cm tall. Estimate its volume in cm³.
practice.hint: One layer is {l} × 5 cubes. The box is 2 layers tall.
practice.explain: {l} × 5 = {=l*5} cubes a layer, and 2 layers make {=l*10}, so about {=l*10} cm³.

practice.prompt: A box is 10 cm long, 10 cm wide and 10 cm tall. How much water fills it?
practice.hint: Work out one layer of 10 × 10 cubes, then 10 layers.
practice.explain: 10 × 10 = 100 cubes a layer, and 10 layers make 1,000 cm³. 1,000 cm³ of water is 1 litre.

pool.prompt: Block A is 3 × 2 × 2 cubes. Block B is 6 × 2 × 1 cubes. Which has the bigger volume?
pool.hint: Count the cubes in each block: one layer, then the layers.
pool.explain: A is 3 × 2 = 6 a layer and 2 layers, so 12. B is 6 × 2 = 12 in one layer. Both are 12 cm³.

pool.prompt: A cuboid is {l} cubes long, {w} cubes wide and 2 cubes tall. How many cubes is it made of?
pool.hint: One layer is {l} × {w}. There are 2 layers.
pool.explain: {l} × {w} = {=l*w} cubes a layer, and 2 layers make {=l*w*2} cubes, so {=l*w*2} cm³.

pool.prompt: Which unit should you use for the volume of a shoebox?
pool.hint: Volume fills space with cubes. Which unit is a cube?
pool.explain: cm³ is a cube 1 cm along each edge, so it measures volume. cm measures length and cm² measures flat area.

pool.prompt: A box is 9.8 cm by 5.1 cm by 4.2 cm. Which is the best estimate of its volume?
pool.hint: Round to 10, 5 and 4. Work out one layer, then the layers.
pool.explain: 10 × 5 = 50 cubes a layer, and 4 layers make about 200 cm³. 19 adds the edges, and 50 is only one layer.

pool.prompt: Which object has a volume of about 300 cm³?
pool.hint: 300 cm³ is less than a litre carton but much more than a matchbox.
pool.explain: A mug holds about 300 ml, which is 300 cm³. A dice is about 4 cm³ and a shoebox is several thousand cm³.

pool.prompt: You pour 4 full 1 litre jugs into a bucket, and half of a 5th jug fills it. About how much does the bucket hold?
pool.hint: Count the full jugs, then add the part of the last jug that went in.
pool.explain: 4 full jugs plus half a jug is about 4 1/2 litres. It is less than 5 because only half of the 5th jug went in.

pool.prompt: How many ml of water fill {n} cm³?
pool.hint: A cube 1 cm each way holds exactly 1 ml of water.
pool.explain: Each cm³ holds 1 ml, so {n} cm³ holds {n} ml.

pool.prompt: Mia says a box 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm has a volume of 12 cm³. What did she do wrong?
pool.hint: How many cubes are in one layer? How many layers are there?
pool.explain: One layer is 4 × 3 = 12 cubes, but the box is 2 layers tall, so the volume is 24 cm³.
